issues.legal_issue: A later suit for specific performance is not barred by the rule against splitting claims when it is founded on a cause of action distinct from the earlier suit for an injunction.
material_facts: The earlier suit sought an injunction against interference with possession after alleged threats to dispossess the plaintiff.
The later suit sought specific performance after the vendor allegedly failed to perform the sale agreement despite a demand to execute the sale deed.
The suits involved different causes of action and different requirements for obtaining the reliefs sought.
issues.conclusion: The later suit for specific performance was not barred by the rule against splitting claims, and no leave to bring that suit was required.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order II Rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the defendant must establish, among other things, that the later suit is based on the same cause of action as the earlier suit and that the plaintiff omitted a relief available on that cause of action. The Constitution Bench in Gurbux Singh v. Bhooralal, AIR 1964 SC 1810, set out these requirements; Virgo Industries (Eng.) P. Ltd. v. Venturetech Solutions P. Ltd., (2013) 1 SCC 625, reaffirmed that identity of causes of action is essential. Similar pleadings do not establish identity of causes of action.

predicates.two_suits_concern_same_transaction: The plaintiff brought one suit for an injunction and another for specific performance concerning the same property and agreement.
predicates.different_claim_triggers: The injunction claim arose from alleged threats to possession, while the specific-performance claim arose from alleged failure to perform the agreement after a demand.
predicates.injunction_suit_precedes_specific_perfor: The plaintiff filed the injunction suit before filing the suit for specific performance.

issues.definition: When two suits concerning the same transaction rest on different claim triggers, an earlier injunction suit does not bar a later specific-performance suit.

issues.legal_issue: A suit for specific performance of an immovable-property sale agreement without a fixed performance date is within limitation when brought within the prescribed period after the plaintiff learns that performance has been refused.
material_facts: The agreement did not fix a date for completion of the sale; it contemplated efforts to transfer the property after the lease period and allowed the parties to agree on the timing of completion.
The vendor was required to take steps to transfer the property after the lease period expired.

The plaintiff alleged that she learned the vendor and an intended purchaser were asserting ownership and attempting to dispossess her, then demanded performance and filed suit within three years of that alleged refusal.
The agreement concerned the sale of immovable property.
issues.conclusion: Time was not the essence of the agreement, and the suit for specific performance was within limitation because it was filed within three years after the plaintiff had notice of refusal to perform.
issues.legal_principle: For a sale of immovable property, time is ordinarily not of the essence unless the agreement, nature of the property, or surrounding circumstances show otherwise. The Court relied on Section 55 of the Contract Act and Gomathinayagam Pillai v. Pallaniswami Nadar, AIR 1967 SC 868; Govind Prasad Chaturvedi v. Hari Dutt Shastri, (1977) 2 SCC 539; Chand Rani v. Kamal Rani, (1993) 1 SCC 519; K.S. Vidyanadam v. Vairavan, (1997) 3 SCC 1; and K. Narendra v. Riviera Apartments (P) Ltd., (1999) 5 SCC 77. Under Article 54 of the Limitation Act, where no performance date is fixed, the limitation period begins when the plaintiff has notice that performance is refused.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and immovable_property_sale_agreement and no_fixed_performance_date and refusal_known_to_plaintiff and suit_filed_within_three_years_of_refusal

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking specific performance of an agreement.
predicates.immovable_property_sale_agreement: The agreement concerns the sale of immovable property.
predicates.no_fixed_performance_date: The agreement does not set a date for completing performance.
predicates.refusal_known_to_plaintiff: The plaintiff learns that the other contracting party has refused to perform the agreement.
predicates.suit_filed_within_three_years_of_refusal: The plaintiff files the suit within three years after learning of the refusal.

issues.definition: A specific-performance suit concerning an immovable-property sale agreement with no fixed performance date is within limitation when filed within three years after the plaintiff learns of refusal.

issues.legal_issue: A first appellate decree granting specific performance on supported factual findings should not be disturbed in a further appeal unless its findings offend settled law, are arbitrary, or are perverse.
material_facts: The first appellate court independently assessed the evidence and found that the plaintiff had paid the full sale consideration, had been placed in possession, and was ready and willing to perform her obligations.
The first appellate court found that the vendor had failed to perform her obligations and that the subsequent purchaser was not a bona fide purchaser whose title defeated the plaintiff's claim.
The further appeal challenged the first appellate court's factual findings, but the Supreme Court found no basis to treat them as contrary to settled law, arbitrary, or perverse.
issues.conclusion: The Court upheld the first appellate court's findings on the merits and its decree granting specific performance and an injunction.
issues.legal_principle: Section 16 of the Specific Relief Act requires a plaintiff seeking specific performance to plead and prove continuous readiness and willingness to perform the plaintiff's obligations. A first appellate court exercising jurisdiction under Section 96 of the Code of Civil Procedure may independently assess the evidence. Because specific performance is discretionary, a further appellate court hearing an appeal under Article 136 should be slow to interfere with a grant based on evidence unless the finding is contrary to settled law, arbitrary, or perverse.

rule.if: appeal_under_article_136_from_first_appellate_decree and specific_performance_granted and evidence_supports_readiness_and_performance and vendor_failed_to_perform and findings_not_arbitrary_or_perverse

predicates.appeal_under_article_136_from_first_appe: The proceeding is a further appeal challenging a decree made by a first appellate court.
predicates.specific_performance_granted: The first appellate court granted specific performance of an agreement.
predicates.evidence_supports_readiness_and_performa: The evidence supports that the plaintiff was ready and willing to perform and carried out the plaintiff's obligations.
predicates.vendor_failed_to_perform: The evidence supports that the vendor failed to perform the vendor's obligations under the agreement.
predicates.findings_not_arbitrary_or_perverse: The challenged findings are not shown to be contrary to settled law, arbitrary, or perverse.

issues.definition: A further appellate court upholds a first appellate decree granting specific performance when the evidence supports the plaintiff's performance and readiness, the vendor failed to perform, and the findings are not arbitrary or perverse.

issues.legal_issue: A subsequent transferee may be directed to join in the conveyance required to give effect to a decree for specific performance.
material_facts: The property had been transferred by the vendor to a subsequent purchaser.
The decree required the vendor to perform the sale agreement with the plaintiff.
The subsequent purchaser held title that needed to be passed on to the plaintiff to complete the conveyance.
issues.conclusion: The direction requiring the vendor and the subsequent purchaser to execute the conveyance was permissible and was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: The proper form of a decree for specific performance is to direct performance of the contract between the vendor and the plaintiff and require the subsequent transferee to join in the conveyance so as to pass the title held by the transferee, without joining in special covenants between the plaintiff and vendor. The Court relied on Lala Durga Prasad v. Lala Deep Chand, AIR 1954 SC 75.

predicates.specific_performance_decree: The court has decreed specific performance of a contract for the property.
predicates.property_transferred_to_subsequent_trans: The vendor transferred the property to another person after entering the contract with the plaintiff.
predicates.transferee_holds_title_needed_for_convey: The subsequent transferee holds title that must be conveyed to the plaintiff to complete the transfer.

issues.definition: When a specific-performance decree concerns property transferred to someone holding title needed for the conveyance, that transferee may be required to join in the conveyance.

issues.legal_issue: The Court may use its power to do substantial justice to order a vendor to refund consideration received from a subsequent purchaser when the decree prevents completion of their sale contract.
material_facts: The vendor received the purchase consideration from the subsequent purchaser under a sale contract.
The decree requiring conveyance to the plaintiff meant that the vendor could not complete the sale to the subsequent purchaser.
The refund dispute was not separately litigated between the vendor and subsequent purchaser, and an additional suit would prolong the dispute.
The Court considered that ordering the refund would not require intricate factual adjudication or prejudice the parties.
issues.conclusion: The Court directed the vendor to refund the consideration to the subsequent purchaser after execution of the conveyance to the plaintiff, invoking its power to do substantial justice.
issues.legal_principle: When a sale contract fails because the seller cannot transfer title, the seller cannot retain the consideration and the parties should, as far as possible, be restored to their original positions unless the contract provides otherwise. The Court invoked Article 142 of the Constitution to do substantial justice in the case and avoid further litigation.

predicates.civil_appeal_before_supreme_court: The proceeding is a civil appeal before the Supreme Court.
predicates.decree_prevents_vendor_from_completing_s: A decree in favor of another purchaser prevents the vendor from completing the later sale.
predicates.vendor_received_consideration_from_subse: The vendor received consideration from the subsequent purchaser for the sale that cannot be completed.
predicates.refund_order_avoids_further_litigation_w: Ordering repayment avoids a further suit and does not prejudice the parties or require intricate factual adjudication.

issues.definition: In a civil appeal, when a decree prevents completion of a later sale for which the vendor received consideration, the vendor may be ordered to refund it if that resolves the matter without prejudice or intricate factual adjudication.
